strengths: Novel encoding mismatch perspective: The two-view analysis (global SVD + token-level SEP) elegantly resolves the paradox of ViTs being low-rank globally yet difficult to distill, providing genuine mechanistic insight rather than just empirical fixes

Thorough experimental validation: Comprehensive evaluation across multiple architectures (ViT-Tiny/Small/Large/Huge, CaiT, Swin, DeiT variants) with extensive ablations on head designs, projector dimensions, and loss weights demonstrating robustness

Critical validation via standalone improvements: Table 7 demonstrates +0.55-0.68% accuracy gains without any teacher, convincingly proving that encoding mismatch is a genuine architectural bottleneck rather than a distillation artifact

Practical utility with minimal complexity: Proposed strategies (post-hoc lifting and width alignment) are simple, architecture-agnostic, and immediately implementable, with strong empirical results (+2.67 to +3.37% combined gains)
Clear presentation: Well-structured progression from analysis to diagnosis to solution; effective visualizations (especially Figures 1-2) that communicate core findings accessibly

Strong empirical consistency: Results are robust across different hyperparameter settings (Table 5 shows stable improvements with λ_feat variation), and generalize across multiple teacher architectures (Table 6)
weaknesses: SEP analysis conceptual clarity: The use of 1D DFT along channels lacks strong justification—channel indices lack inherent frequency semantics. The claim that this 'reveals' per-token encoding behavior is somewhat interpretive; simpler direct statistics (e.g., per-token effective rank) might be more fundamental than frequency-domain framing

Limited scope of evaluation: Experiments confined to ImageNet-1K classification only. Generalization to other vision tasks (detection, segmentation) or modalities unknown. No wall-clock timing/efficiency analysis for Strategy 1's added projector parameters and computation at inference

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: The paper documents but does not explain why SEP curves are universal across vastly different architectures (192-1280 channels, 12-32 layers). Additionally, Table 6 puzzle remains: why does CaiT-S24 (384-dim) distill better than DeiT-Small (also 384-dim) if encoding mismatch is the primary factor?

Missing statistical rigor and comparisons: No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple random seeds reported. Recent ViT distillation methods (ViTKD, VKD, SpectralKD) are cited but not empirically compared in tables. Results appear to be single runs, limiting reproducibility assessment

Methods lack novelty: Post-hoc projectors and width matching are straightforward techniques. Contribution is primarily in understanding why existing approaches work rather than proposing novel methods. Analysis is the main contribution, limiting methodological impact

Incomplete exploration of generalization: Unclear if approach applies to very large models (ViT-Huge+). Intermediate layer distillation not explored—does encoding mismatch persist throughout the network or only at final layer? Boundary conditions and failure cases not discussed

Weak causal evidence: While encoding mismatch is plausible and correlational evidence is strong, counterfactual tests are limited (e.g., varying student width gradually to see if distillation follows predicted curve). Standalone improvements provide strongest causal evidence but are modest (+0.55-0.68%)

Unexplored channel utilization patterns: The paper shows tokens use most channels but doesn't analyze whether preferred channels exist, whether usage is random/uniform, or whether different tokens use overlapping/disjoint subsets—deeper analysis could strengthen mechanistic claims

strengths: Well-articulated paradox: identifies genuine puzzle that ViT features are globally low-rank (suggesting simple projector should work) yet feature KD fails empirically
Thorough empirical analysis: SVD analysis across multiple architectures with rigorous statistical reporting (99th-percentile, means, standard deviations over 1000 images)
Complementary dual perspectives: SVD and SEP together provide intuitive two-view characterization of the problem
Standalone validation: Table 7 shows improvements without teacher signal (+0.55%, +0.68%), strengthening claim that encoding mismatch is architectural bottleneck rather than distillation artifact
Reproducibility: full training details, paired experimental design, extensive appendix with per-model analysis
Clear presentation: well-written with good visualizations and comprehensive appendix
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: proposed methods are trivial consequences of diagnosis (Strategy 1 adds a linear projector, Strategy 2 widens last block)—both are straightforward architectural modifications without novel mechanisms

Arbitrary analysis design: SEP applies 1D DFT to channel dimension despite channels lacking inherent frequency structure; justification is circular ('treats frequency axis simply as consistent index'). Direct per-token rank metric would be more principled

Narrow evaluation scope: only ImageNet-1K classification tested; no results on other datasets, tasks (detection/segmentation), or modalities despite mentioning them in conclusion; limited architectural generality

Weak baseline comparisons: insufficient comparison with recent ViT KD methods (ViTKD, VKD, ScaleKD, etc.); SpectralKD baseline shows only +0.21 improvement, but no analysis of whether these methods already address width mismatch; missing state-of-the-art comparisons

Insufficient mechanistic understanding: paper observes tokens spread energy diagonally across channels but doesn't explain WHY; causality between encoding mismatch and KD failure not rigorously established; alternative explanations (attention patterns, gradient flow) not ruled out

Incomplete method analysis: Strategy 1 inference overhead (added parameters/FLOPs) not discussed; Strategy 2 design space not explored (why only widen last block? not thorough); improvements lack statistical significance testing (single runs, no error bars)
Arbitrary threshold choices: 99th-percentile rank, 99%/95%/90%/80% energy thresholds lack justification; sensitivity analysis missing
Low per-token analysis depth: while SEP computed per token, distribution variance not reported; no breakdown of which tokens are bottlenecks
Statistical rigor concerns: Table 7 standalone improvements (+0.55%, +0.68%) relatively small; no confidence intervals or multiple runs reported
Missing ablations: LayerNorm in loss function (Eq. 7-8) not standard—contribution not ablated; loss weight selection (λ_logit, λ_feat) appears ad-hoc

strengths: Novel and insightful diagnosis of ViT distillation failure: The encoding mismatch framework elegantly resolves the paradox of globally low-rank yet hard-to-distill representations through complementary SVD and SEP analyses

Comprehensive empirical analysis: Extensive SVD analysis across 6 architectures with consistent findings; SEP analysis reveals striking universality in token encoding patterns (b₉₀% ≈ 0.9); proper statistical treatment with 99th percentiles and distributions

Strong experimental validation: Substantial improvements (74.86% → 78.23% for DeiT-Tiny); thorough ablations on head types, projector dimensions, and loss weights; generalization demonstrated across multiple teachers
Practical and interpretable solutions: Both proposed strategies are minimal, architecture-agnostic, and easy to implement; provide clear design guidance for compact ViTs
High reproducibility: Complete training protocol, standard benchmarks (ImageNet-1K), extensive appendix with per-model details, and public model implementations used

Clear and well-organized presentation: Logical flow from diagnosis to solution, effective visualizations, particularly Figures 1-2 that clearly communicate the low-rank vs. high per-token utilization paradox
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in proposed methods: Both strategies (post-hoc projector, widening last block) are straightforward architectural modifications. The contribution is primarily analytical rather than methodological, with solutions being direct applications of the diagnosis

Incomplete causal link between SEP and distillation difficulty: While the paper shows tokens use broad channel bandwidth, the mechanistic explanation of why this hurts narrow students lacks rigor. No formal analysis of optimization dynamics or what narrow students actually learn under MSE loss

Questionable SEP methodology: Using DFT along channel dimension is unconventional; alternatives (information-theoretic measures, per-token dimensionality analysis) are not compared or justified. SEP analysis limited to last layer only; behavior across layers and during training unexplored

Narrow experimental scope: Evaluation limited to ImageNet-1K classification only; no other datasets, tasks, or modalities. Width-ratio exploration limited to 2× (192→384). Critically, missing quantitative comparisons with recent ViT distillation methods (VitKD, VKD, ScaleKD, etc.) - only SpectralKD compared

Unaddressed inference-time costs: Strategy 1 retains projector at inference, adding parameters and computation overhead in a compression pipeline. Trade-off against Strategy 2 not discussed or quantified

Weak validation of 'genuine architectural bottleneck' claim: Standalone improvements (+0.55%/+0.68%, Table 7) are small and lack error bars or multiple runs. Alternative explanations (larger final-layer dimension helps generally) not ruled out. Conclusion's claim of 'genuine bottleneck' appears overstated
Theory-experiment contradiction: Table 4 shows 448D projector slightly outperforms teacher-matched 384D, contradicting the theory that matching teacher width is optimal

Incomplete related work: Limited engagement with width scaling literature; unclear if observation that wider final layers help is fundamentally novel or known principle; recent projector-based distillation insufficiently reviewed

strengths: Novel diagnostic framework combining sample-wise SVD, dataset-level PCA, and Spectral Energy Pattern analysis that elegantly decomposes the feature-KD failure mechanism, revealing the 'low-rank yet hard to distill' paradox
Exceptionally comprehensive empirical validation across 14+ architectures (supervised, self-supervised, multimodal) with consistent patterns and detailed appendices (Figures 3-15, Tables 1, 8)

Significant practical improvements with strong results: DeiT-Tiny from CaiT-S24 improves from 74.86% to 77.53%/78.23%, with consistent gains across different feature losses (MSE, SpectralKD, combined objectives)

Rigorous experimental methodology: thorough ablations on classifier heads, projector dimensions, and loss weights; generalization across multiple teachers; standalone performance gains validating the architectural bottleneck hypothesis
Practical and interpretable solutions directly motivated by analysis: Lift and WideLast are simple, minimal modifications that are easy to adopt and understand without requiring complex redesigns
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figures 1-2) that compellingly convey main insights; honest discussion of limitations and open questions
weaknesses: Limited experimental scope: evaluation restricted to ImageNet-1K with primarily DeiT-Tiny→CaiT-S24 pairs (4.3× compression). Unclear generalization to other datasets (CIFAR-100, downstream tasks), extreme compression ratios (384→64), or diverse student-teacher configurations

Theoretical gaps in SEP analysis: (1) DFT on channels assumes problematic sequential structure; (2) 'why tokens spread energy uniformly' is observed but unexplained; (3) connection between high SEP bandwidth and actual distillation difficulty is intuitive but not rigorously established; (4) diagonal pattern on normalized axes may be circular for random signals
Analysis limited to last-layer features only; no investigation of whether encoding mismatch affects intermediate layers or is last-layer-specific, despite being acknowledged as valuable future work

Limited novelty in proposed methods: lifting projectors in distillation are known techniques; width expansion is straightforward. While empirically effective, solutions are somewhat incremental. Novelty lies primarily in diagnosis rather than methodology

Incomplete comparison with related work: ScaleKD, VkD, and RSD mentioned but not experimentally compared. No head-to-head evaluation against existing alignment-based approaches to establish relative efficiency and effectiveness

Missing practical details: no inference latency/FLOPs analysis for Lift overhead; WideLast requires architectural modifications—unclear implications for pretrained model loading; only last layer widening tested; behavior under extreme compression ratios unknown

Reproducibility concerns: dataset PCA based on 1,000 validation images with unstated sensitivity; specific per-architecture hyperparameters not detailed; sensitivity analysis on energy thresholds (95%, 99%) absent
Architectural specificity unclear: whether findings are ViT-specific or apply to CNNs unexplored; why feature KD works in CNNs if similar phenomena occur is not addressed

strengths: Well-motivated diagnosis of the 'encoding mismatch' paradox through complementary SVD/PCA/SEP analysis that clearly articulates why per-image compressibility does not guarantee good feature distillation
Comprehensive empirical analysis demonstrating the phenomenon across diverse ViT architectures and training regimes (Table 1), strengthening universality claims
Clear presentation with compelling visualizations (Figures 1-2) and thorough appendices providing supporting diagnostics across 14+ models
Practical improvements with simple fixes: +3.37% on CaiT-S24→DeiT-Tiny and consistent standalone performance gains (Table 7) validating the architectural bottleneck diagnosis
Extensive ablations (Tables 3-5) on design choices, demonstrating robustness to classifier heads, projector dimensions, and loss weights
weaknesses: Solutions are incremental engineering fixes (add projector, widen layer) rather than conceptual innovations; given the diagnosis, these remedies are straightforward and obvious, limiting novelty

Incomplete causal explanation: the paper diagnoses two failure modes (rotation + bandwidth) but does not prove these mechanisms drive KD failure; connection between SEP's high per-token bandwidth and actual KD failure is inferred rather than rigorously established

Critical empirical gaps: (1) only ImageNet-1K evaluated; (2) no comparison to recent competing ViT-KD methods (ScaleKD, VkD, SpectralKD, RSD) despite citing them; (3) much smaller improvements on other teachers (+0.96-1.64% vs. +3.37% for CaiT-S24), suggesting limited generalization

WideLast's claimed 'input-dependent expansion' for subspace rotation is asserted but not validated; no analysis shows the widened last block actually learns to adapt to rotating subspaces across inputs

Overclaimed universality of SEP: (a) variance visible in Table 8 (e.g., ViT-Small DINO b₅₀%=0.477 vs. others ≈0.50); (b) all experiments on ViTs; generalization to CNNs or hybrids untested; (c) frequency-domain choice for 'bandwidth' is intuitive but not justified against alternatives

Missing analysis of proposed solutions: no computational cost comparison for Lift's inference projector, no efficiency-accuracy tradeoffs, no exploration of why fixes work differently across teacher architectures

Methodological gaps: SEP uses 1D DFT but alternative measures of per-token compressibility (effective dimension, ℓ₂ ratios) are not explored; uncentered PCA choice in Eq. 4 lacks justification; no error bars or multi-run statistics
Limited scope of applicability not discussed: behavior when teacher is also narrow, performance when teacher/student widths are comparable, applicability beyond classification

strengths: Rigorous three-pronged diagnostic analysis (SVD+PCA+SEP) with novel spectral energy patterns perspective that provides genuine mechanistic insight into feature-map distillation failure
Exceptional empirical breadth across 15+ architectures (ViT, CaiT, DeiT, Swin, DINO, MAE, CLIP variants) with consistent findings, demonstrating universality of encoding mismatch phenomenon
Clear articulation of paradox: per-image compressibility vs. dataset-level non-low-rankness with effective visualization in Figure 1
Strong experimental validation including Table 7 demonstrating improvements without distillation, proving encoding mismatch is genuine architectural bottleneck rather than training artifact
Simple, interpretable, and practical solutions (Lift and WideLast) well-motivated by analysis without requiring complex engineering
Comprehensive ablation studies examining head types, projector dimensions, and loss weights demonstrating robustness of approach
High-quality presentation with clear writing and effective figures; thorough supplementary materials with per-model diagnostics across architectures
weaknesses: Lack of theoretical grounding: paper empirically observes universal SEP diagonal pattern but provides no principled explanation for why this emerges across diverse architectures or how it relates to fundamental properties of Transformer representations

Limited novelty in proposed solutions: Lift is essentially learned linear projection and WideLast is straightforward 'widen last layer'—solutions are incremental architectural tweaks once problem is diagnosed
Scope restricted to image classification (ImageNet-1K); unclear whether findings generalize to detection, segmentation, or other dense prediction tasks
Analysis focuses exclusively on final layer; acknowledged but unaddressed intermediate layer investigation limits understanding of when/where feature-map KD fails
Technical justification for uncentered PCA (Eq. 4) is post-hoc; standard centered PCA is conventional and deserves explanation beyond energy-matching convenience

Incomplete causal analysis: relationships between subspace rotation, high per-token bandwidth, and per-image compressibility are documented but causal interplay remains unclear; unable to isolate which factor drives failure
Limited empirical comparison with concurrent methods (ScaleKD, VkD, RSD, Redundancy Suppression) in main results; only discussed in related work
Inference cost of Lift (192→384 projection per token) not quantified; practical overhead at deployment time unaddressed
Ambiguity in SEP interpretation: diagonal pattern could simply reflect universal importance of all frequency components rather than evidence of fundamental bandwidth requirements
Table 4 finding underexplored: projector width 448D (exceeding teacher) hurts standalone performance, contradicting capacity-focused narrative and suggesting misalignment also matters
